proposals.relationship: Portelli uses Gramsci’s organic-intellectual concept to explain intellectual responsibility as learning from popular worlds and carrying their voices into public discourse.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview with Paulo Álvarez Bravo in Santiago, 4 December 2015, published 2017. Portelli invokes Gramsci but separately credits mentor Gianni Bosio’s inverted intellectual and the agency of narrators; neither Bosio nor those narrators are replaced by a generic Gramscian lineage. This is a specified conceptual use, not a claim that Gramsci founded oral history. The interview prints Bossio; the established Gianni Bosio identity is retained. Gramsci’s original text was not freshly read.
primary_locators: Kamchatka 9(2017), printed 546, section Los intelectuales, Portelli’s answer beginning Hay todo tipo de intelectuales, with continuation 547. Interview date in n 1,p 544.

proposals.relationship: Sangster explicitly takes Portelli as a guide for interpreting what working people wanted, believed and later made of their experiences, alongside the events themselves.
proposals.evidence_note: Sangster’s own 2013 account links this resource to attention to subjectivity and the interview relationship. She also rejects an overly simple progression from naive recovery to sophisticated interpretation; this is not a claim that meaning replaces evidence or that Portelli supplied every element of her approach. The article’s body misspells his given name as Alexandro, but n 27 identifies Alessandro Portelli’s 1991 essay and p 50. The 2014 reader version and the 2013 journal article are distinct; the proposed witness is the actual journal PDF.
primary_locators: Oral History Forum d’histoire orale 33(2013), printed 8 first paragraph, Taking Alexandro Portelli as a guide, and n 27; read with 7 and 9–10 on earlier memory work and the limits of a Whig narrative.

proposals.relationship: As Malena reproduces Portelli’s recollection, Ginzburg criticized his early Terni manuscript for explanations that reduced the richness of the narrators’ stories; Portelli thought the criticism right.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Adelisa Malena’s 2016 essay,p 176 and n 54, follows Alessandro Casellato’s 2014 discussion and reproduces Portelli’s 1987 recollection. Cesare Bermani and Liliana Lanzardo retain their roles in that original conversation. Neither the 1987 original nor Ginzburg’s manuscript comments were freshly read. This is a particular editorial/methodological criticism, not rejection of oral history or evidence that all Portelli’s practice descends from microhistory. A separate 2022 own interview confirms the Ginzburg/Microstorie connection without independently reproducing this criticism.
primary_locators: Malena, The sound of silence, printed 176, paragraph introducing Casellato followed by the indented Portelli quotation and n 54; bibliography 183 identifies Bermani–Lanzardo–Portelli 1987,pp 23–27.
